prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, and its development to accuracy and stability at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B042 with Katori and Ye. Having read all eight statements, I think the chair's first question can be answered concretely. The new principle is not precision metrology in general but a specific idea: choosing the trap wavelength so that the light shift of the clock transition cancels, which lets thousands of neutral atoms sit in a Lamb-Dicke lattice with no Doppler or recoil broadening. That is different in kind from the 2005 comb, which made optical frequencies countable, and from the 2012 prize, which rested on control of one ion or one photon and therefore on a single-particle signal. Many atoms interrogated in parallel are what give the stability that makes 10^-18 systematics measurable in practice, and the architecture has been reproduced in Sr, Yb and Hg in several laboratories and compared across continents. The citation should rest on both the concept (Katori) and the demonstrated performance (Ye), because neither alone is the achievement, and it should claim nothing about the pending redefinition of the second or the thorium nuclear clock. Kroll and Lindroth reach the same two names from the atomic side. Lindroth and the chair's question warn that agreement among atomic-physics members may be a shared vantage, so I note that my own field is circuit theory, not atomic physics. I read the clock case as mature, with the cleanest two-person credit on the list, and as the configuration with no decisive scientific objection that has survived round 1.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is the one Pearce and Danielsson press: this extends a measurement capability whose earlier steps were honoured in 2005 and 2012, and it answers no question comparable to the origin of mass or the opening of a new observational channel. I accept that is a judgement about the kind of achievement, and a reasonable committee could weigh it differently from me. Second, a two-name prize leaves out Takamoto and Ido, who made the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration, and Lemonde, Ludlow and others. I cannot say the supplied evidence settles whether their claim is equal to Ye's, and the citation can only be careful, not complete. Third, Ye's reputation also rests on comb and laser-stabilisation work, so his credit must be confined to the lattice clock.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the Higgs discovery answers a half-century question, that the 2013 prize covered only the theory, and that if no defensible three names exist the committee should turn elsewhere; he also doubts that precision metrology answers a comparable question.
responses.response: I agree with his conditional: if no defensible three names exist, the committee should turn elsewhere, and in my view that condition is met here. His own concession that spokespersons and analysis leaders have a competing claim is the problem. In round 1 he describes the trio as founding proposers and leaders, yet the discovery was made by analysis teams, so a citation can credit conception and leadership but not the observation itself. I do not dispute the 2013 point; the experiment is a separate achievement, and I have moved B026 up to an alternative. But a clean claim for the science is not the same as a clean claim for three people, and I would not set aside the cleaner two-name case on that basis alone.

responses.point: Pearce prefers IceCube with Halzen and Spiering as a genuinely new observational channel and regards the clocks as a refinement of capabilities that the 2005 and 2012 prizes created, while accepting B042 as his first alternative.
responses.response: His distinction between a new channel and a refinement is a fair test, and I think the clocks pass it on the point I would apply: a different measurement principle, not a better implementation of an old one. The comb and single-ion work did not provide many-atom light-shift-free interrogation. I take the other side of his caution on IceCube: the diffuse flux is secure but he lists partial source identification and the Baikal and DUMAND pioneers himself, and I cannot judge the astrophysics. I note his Fermi-LAT disclosure on B029 and agree that recusal there is for the committee, but I do not need his case to be disqualified for my conclusion. His own statement that he would be comfortable with B042 is what I would build on.

responses.point: Mehlig asks what new principle the lattice clock adds beyond a superb implementation, accepts the magic-wavelength concept with many-atom Lamb-Dicke interrogation as a fair claim, and also proposes Blais rather than Girvin as the theorist in B033.
responses.response: The principle he names is the one I would put in the citation, and I take it as an answer to the chair's question from a member outside AMO. On B033 his reasoning for Blais over Girvin is sound as physics, and it shows the three-name subset is a real decision, which is why I no longer carry that case. Because I direct WACQT and work in this very field, I would recuse on B033 and do not want my view of the allocation to count. I do not move to B034: KPZ is beautifully confirmed, but I cannot check the attribution against Parisi and the exact-solution authors, and with only a single member preferring it I would need other statistical-physics members to say it is the strongest case.

responses.point: Kroll would credit Ye strictly for the strontium lattice clock and its record comparisons, keep the thorium nuclear clock out of the citation, and treats B053 as the fallback while noting the experimental credit is shared across ion groups.
responses.response: I agree on the boundary for Ye: lattice clock and its comparisons, and the thorium work stays out. I would reflect that in the wording, which names the concept and the 10^-18 performance but not the redefinition. On B053 his objection about the experimental credit is correct, and it is why I place B053 only as an alternative. I also take his point that the 2005 and 2012 history could be read either way, so I will not defend the timing as natural, only as consistent.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B042 first and warns that agreement among members with an atomic-physics vantage is not itself evidence of merit; she says B026 could outrank it if it received a defensible attribution.
responses.response: Her warning is right and I take it seriously. It is why I have restated the argument in terms of the measurement principle and not the vote count. We share the Lemonde and Takamoto concern, and the best I can offer is a citation written around the concept and the demonstrated performance so that it claims no more than the two names delivered. I agree with her that B026 is the case that could change my mind, but only if a member names a principle and each person's concrete role, and nobody has done so in round 1.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto, Ido or Lemonde have a priority claim that a two-name citation cannot cover, and whether the committee should accept that omission.
Whether members outside atomic physics will treat light-shift cancellation with many-atom interrogation as a new principle, as I do, or as a refinement of work honoured in 2005 and 2012.
Whether a defensible principle for three names in B026 can still be stated, since the committee would then have a stronger scientific case than mine.
I am not an atomic physicist, so my assessment of the individual roles of Katori and Ye relies on the supplied evidence and my general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: I work in circuit and waveguide QED, direct WACQT at Chalmers, and have close Chalmers links to Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent collaboration with Anton Frisk Kockum. I would recuse from B033, which I no longer prefer, and I have not argued for it. Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. Olsson has noted that I am a Chalmers colleague; I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye, and none to the B053 or B026 names.
